The letter to ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ is the third of the pastoral letters, and it belongs to the same late chapter of ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s life as the first letter to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧. Once again Paul writes to a trusted colleague he has left behind to finish a task. This time the place is not a great city but an island: ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧, the long, mountainous island that lies across the southern edge of the Aegean Sea, south of mainland ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧.

⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ never appears by name in Acts, but ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s other letters show how much he relied on him. Titus was a Greek, a Gentile convert. On one visit to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ he went up with Paul and ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧, and Paul later pointed out that the leaders there had not required him to be circumcised. Years afterwards Titus was Paul's envoy to the troubled church in ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, sent to learn how they had taken a painful letter, bringing back news that comforted Paul greatly, and helping to organise the collection for the poor in Jerusalem. He was the colleague Paul sent where firmness and tact were both needed.

How the gospel first reached ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧ is not recorded. Cretans were among the crowd in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ on the day of Pentecost, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s ship called briefly at a harbour on the island on the voyage to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ that ends Acts, but neither moment describes the founding of churches. This letter simply tells us that Paul and ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ had worked in Crete together, that Paul had moved on, and that Titus had stayed to put in order what remained unfinished and to appoint elders in every town. As with the letters to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, the visit belongs to the years after Paul's first imprisonment in Rome.

The churches in ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧ were young and unsettled. There were rebellious talkers in them, especially among those of the circumcision group, who were teaching for gain, upsetting whole households, and promoting myths, genealogies and quarrels about the law. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ quotes a line from a Cretan poet, Epimenides, about the island's people being liars, a jibe the ancient world knew well. ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ was to answer this by appointing sound leaders, by teaching clearly, and by showing what a well-ordered Christian life looked like in a place where reputations mattered.

The letter is short, and its three chapters move in a natural order. The first concerns elders and the false teachers they will have to resist. The second turns to the households of the church, older men and women, younger men and women, and slaves, and grounds their way of life in the grace of God that has appeared in Christ. The third widens to the believers' conduct as citizens and neighbours, recalls how God saved them, and ends with travel plans.

Those plans are a small window onto ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s world in motion. He intends to send ⟦p:artemas_315|Artemas⟧ or ⟦p:tychicus_2885|Tychicus⟧ to take ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧'s place, and asks Titus to join him at ⟦l:nicopolis_894|Nicopolis⟧, on the western coast of ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, where Paul has decided to spend the winter. The second letter to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ will later mention, in passing, that Titus has gone on to Dalmatia, across the Adriatic, in what is now Croatia.
1:
The letter opens with one of the longest greetings in ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s letters, a full sentence about his calling as a servant of God and an apostle, and about the hope of eternal life promised before time began. Only then does he name ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧, his true child in a common faith.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ moves at once to the task. He reminds ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ why he was left in ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧: to set in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town. The qualities he describes are much like those in the first letter to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, with the same weight on character, household and self-control, and on holding firmly to sound teaching.

That last point leads to the reason it matters. Many in the Cretan churches are rebellious and full of empty talk, especially some from among the Jewish believers, and they are upsetting whole households for the sake of money. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ quotes the Cretan poet's harsh line about his own people, and tells ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ to rebuke such teachers sharply, so that the churches may be sound in the faith.
2:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has described the false teachers in ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧, whose lives contradict what they claim to believe. Now he turns to ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧, and to what he should teach instead. The contrast is deliberate. Over against empty talk and corrupted households, Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine, and to show it in ordinary life.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ goes through the church group by group: older men, older women, who are to train the younger women, younger men, ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ himself, and slaves. Throughout, he keeps one eye on outsiders. He wants nothing in the believers' lives to bring the message into disrepute, and he wants their conduct to make the teaching about God attractive. In a world that judged a new religion largely by the households it produced, that mattered.

Then the chapter rises to its centre. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ explains why such a life is possible, and what it looks back to and forward to: the grace of God that has appeared, and the hope of the glorious appearing of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧, who gave himself to redeem and purify a people for his own. He closes by telling ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ to teach these things with authority, and to let no one despise him.
3:
The previous chapter spoke of the household. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ now widens the view to the believers' place in the wider community. He asks ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ to remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be ready for every good work, and to be gentle and courteous to everyone. ⟦l:crete_310|Crete⟧ was a Roman province, and Christians there, as elsewhere, were watched by neighbours who knew little about them.

To ground this, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ recalls what he and his readers once were, foolish and enslaved to their desires, and then sets out in a few compact lines how God saved them, not because of their own righteous deeds, but by his mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.

The letter then returns briefly to the troublemakers, with instructions on how to deal with a divisive person, before closing with the travel plans for ⟦l:nicopolis_894|Nicopolis⟧ and a request that ⟦p:titus_2869|Titus⟧ help two travellers on their way: Zenas the lawyer, and ⟦p:apollos_276|Apollos⟧, the learned teacher from ⟦l:alexandria_46|Alexandria⟧ whom Acts and the letters to ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧ remember well.
